title: Maria Ressa on AI overreliance: ‘Don’t outsource the nuances’
summary: ‘You can do it faster, but can you do it?’ Maria Ressa says in an interview with Rappler, cautioning young learners against relying on AI to do their work

‘You can do it faster, but can you do it?’ Maria Ressa says in an interview with Rappler, cautioning young learners against relying on AI to do their work

items: Maria Ressa emphasizes the need for balance, acknowledging that while AI can enhance efficiency, it should not replace essential skills and independent thinking.
She highlights the dangers of chatbots, which can create emotional dependence and blur the lines between fact and fiction.

MANILA, Philippines – Rappler chief executive officer and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa warned that growing overreliance on artificial intelligence could weaken critical thinking and harm newsrooms, one of the pillars of democratic societies.

In an interview with Rappler, Ressa discussed how chatbots can “hack” one’s biology, as they’re designed to keep users engaged, even when it may ultimately dull their ability to think and work independently.

“If you use that chatbot to do your assignment, you could get a good grade, but you won’t learn to think,” she said on the sidelines of the ASEAN Business and Investment Summit on Sunday, November 15.

“It’s anthropomorphic, meaning it pretends to be real, like a human being,” Ressa added. “It’s also sycophantic by design, meaning you actually have to tell it to counter you, or else it tells you what it sees you want to hear.”

That is a damaging combination that Ressa points out has already led to real-life harm, citing the case of Sewell Setzer III, a 14-year-old who took his own life after developing emotional dependence on a Character.AI chatbot. His mother subsequently sued the company, alleging that the chatbot contributed to her son’s death.

blocks.text: AI can also damage newsrooms, with Ressa saying that the proliferation of chatbots and AI content is “part of the reason that you can’t tell the difference between fact and fiction,” contributing to the degradation of democracy.
“The world is a world of nuance. It is a world of learning. Don’t outsource the nuances,” Ressa told Rappler, speaking about how AI is changing the newsroom.

But it’s not all doom and gloom. Ressa acknowledged that AI can have its place in the newsroom. Rappler, for example, has introduced an AI-driven summary on top of its stories to help readers quickly understand the news and context.
The lesson here is one of balance. While AI can certainly accelerate work, an overreliance on it can prevent people from developing the skills needed to actually accomplish their job.
“What happens to this next generation that doesn’t develop the skills that are necessary, to actually be able to pull up and think with clarity?” Ressa said.
“You can do it faster, but can you do it?” – Rappler.com
